Theorem (1 + 1.75) on the Goldbach conjecture

Ruiyi Zhang Independent Researcher, Columbia, Maryland, USA
(Date: November 13, 2026)
Abstract.

Every sufficiently large even integer NN has a representation N=p+r⁢qN=p+rq, where p,qp,q are prime, r=1r=1 or prime, and r≤qa−1=q3/4r\leq q^{a-1}=q^{3/4}. In the terminology of Li and Liu, this proves Proposition (1+a)(1+a) for a=1.75=7/4a=1.75=7/4. A weighted sieve combines thirteen signed row estimates with a switched upper bound. The directed comparison gives DB>1.967088903489691335582703173494D_{B}>1.967088903489691335582703173494 and cK⁢2,G⁢0⁢I⁢(b)<1.966859949178424046530804965344c_{K2,G0}I(b)<1.966859949178424046530804965344. The exact margin enclosure is DB−cK⁢2,G⁢0⁢I⁢(b)>0.000228954311267289051898208151D_{B}-c_{K2,G0}I(b)>0.000228954311267289051898208151.

Key words and phrases:
Goldbach problem, sieve methods, primes in arithmetic progressions, automorphic forms

Primary 11P32; Secondary 11N36, 11N35

1. Introduction

We represent large even integers by two primes and one factor. Write ℙ\mathbb{P} for the primes. Chen’s theorem represents every sufficiently large even integer as a prime plus an integer with at most two prime factors [5]. Paper II supplies the quantitative smaller-factor starting point and the signed sieve sums used here. We change the exterior and switched coefficients and add retained and sixth-sum gains. Table 1.1 lists their separate costs. We use the terminology Proposition (1+a)(1+a) introduced by Li and Liu [19, p. 2, (1.6)]. Runbo Li proved lower bounds for D1,2⁢(N)D_{1,2}(N) [29]; we do not use that result.

Cai established a small-prime variant of Chen’s theorem [4]. Wu developed Chen’s double sieve for Goldbach and twin-prime problems [30]. His later paper continues this double-sieve program [31]. Lichtman modified the linear sieve and studied bounds for the twin-prime counting function [20]. He also proved results on large-modulus distribution and Goldbach beyond the square-root barrier [21]. Maynard’s first paper proves large-modulus estimates for fixed residue classes [22]. His second gives well-factorable estimates in that setting [23]. His third treats estimates uniform over residue classes [24]. Pascadi studies exponents of distribution for primes and smooth numbers [28]. Li and Liu proved Proposition (1+1.9)(1+1.9), with a lower bound for D1,1.9⁢(N)D_{1,1.9}(N) [19, Theorem 1.1]. The present proof does not use their estimates.

Theorem 1 (Representation theorem).

Let σ∗\sigma_{*} be a rational number satisfying (9.14), and let N0∗⁢(σ∗)N_{0}^{*}(\sigma_{*}) be the threshold (2.5). Then every even N≥N0∗⁢(σ∗)N\geq N_{0}^{*}(\sigma_{*}) admits

(1.1) N=p+r⁢q,p,q∈ℙ,r∈{1}∪ℙ,r≤qa−1=q3/4.N=p+rq,\qquad p,q\in\mathbb{P},\qquad r\in\{1\}\cup\mathbb{P},\qquad r\leq q^{% a-1}=q^{3/4}.

Section 5 proves the retained comparison (A1) of Table 1.2. Section 6 proves the sixth-sum estimate (A2). Section 7 proves the exterior comparison (A3). Section 8 proves the switched comparison (A4). The constant bounds (A5) follow from the cited Paper I and Paper II estimates, including Paper I, Theorem 2.6, (2.31) [26, Theorem 2.6, (2.31)]. Hence a rational σ∗\sigma_{*} as in the theorem exists; N0∗⁢(σ∗)N_{0}^{*}(\sigma_{*}) may be ineffective.

The proof uses Paper I, [26, Theorems 2.6, 2.8, 3.2 and 4.1], and Paper II, [27, (1.7)–(1.12), (6.4)–(6.4d)]. We restate each input below with its precise scope.

The common threshold is defined in (2.5). It includes every length, structural and error threshold. Every limit is taken at fixed σ∗\sigma_{*}. Each requirement includes its exact nonnegative error estimates and the fixed-σ∗\sigma_{*} limits allocated in Section 9. The source-counting identity and pointwise bound are supplied in Section 4. The list only records dependencies. The cited sections prove the estimates, with precise scopes and error bounds; the scalar arithmetic here combines them.

The use of AI tools is described at the end.

2. Notation and parameters

All logarithms are natural. Put L=log⁡NL=\log N. The integer NN is even throughout. Table 2.1 fixes the common notation.

Cusps carry the index 𝔞\mathfrak{a} in spectral sums. The switched blocks carry the index 𝔟\mathfrak{b}. Partition cells are cc or 𝔠\mathfrak{c}. Coefficient sequences are an,bma_{n},b_{m}, with dummy indices interchanged when needed. Spectral moduli and cusp numerators are locally bound variables. They do not redefine the constants cc and uu. Packing coordinates also have local scope. Bare TT and ww are local endpoints or weights; the named saved and root-A scales are Tsave,TintT_{\mathrm{save}},T_{\mathrm{int}}, and wRAw_{\mathrm{RA}}. The exponent A0>0A_{0}>0 in distribution estimates is a logarithmic precision. The normalization factor is written 2⁢e−γ2e^{-\gamma}.

3. Classical inputs

We use counting-measure ℓ2\ell^{2} norms. Write n∼Yn\sim Y for Y<n≤2⁢YY<n\leq 2Y. The symbols μMob,Λ,φ\mu_{\rm Mob},\Lambda,\varphi have their usual meanings. Write d⁢(n)d(n) for the divisor function. The parameters in each fact are local. Put P−⁢(1)=∞P^{-}(1)=\infty and e⁢(t)=exp⁡(2⁢π⁢i⁢t)e(t)=\exp(2\pi it). Statements (P1.x) and (P2.x) restate results proved in Papers I and II, respectively, with their original scope. The structured sieve result is Paper I, Theorem 2.6. Its classical source is Iwaniec’s Theorem 4 [13, Theorem 4]. The SS-form displayed below specializes the WR±W_{R}^{\pm} estimates of Paper I, Theorem 2.6. It follows from them by S≤WR+S\leq W_{R}^{+} and S≥WR−S\geq W_{R}^{-}. Theorem 4 does not state it verbatim. Each new application needs its own coefficient, support and uniformity checks.

Fact 3.13 ((F12) Eisenstein inputs).

Paper I uses three classical Eisenstein properties. The Eisenstein family has a meromorphic continuation, which allows compact Fourier-coefficient extraction. It has an arithmetic Fourier normalization. There is a complete irredundant cusp set. For the cusp u/wu/w, let ddend_{\rm den} be the lower-row denominator variable in c⁢z+ddencz+d_{\rm den} and write the printed variable as d=−ddend=-d_{\rm den}. The printed denominator is therefore c⁢z−dcz-d, and the Fourier phase changes with this sign choice. Thus replacing dd by −d-d changes the congruence and the phase together, not one sign in isolation. The normalization includes the orbit conditions

(c,d)=1,(c,q)=w,c⁢d≡u⁢w(mod(w2,q)).(c,d)=1,\quad(c,q)=w,\quad cd\equiv uw\pmod{(w^{2},q)}.

With c=w⁢γc=w\gamma, the last condition is γ⁢d≡u(mod(w,q/w))\gamma d\equiv u\pmod{(w,q/w)}. The cusp set has the form

u/w,w∣q,u(mod(w,q/w)),(u,(w,q/w))=1,u/w,\quad w\mid q,\quad u\pmod{(w,q/w)},\quad(u,(w,q/w))=1,

with admissible lifts chosen coprime to qq. The sources are Iwaniec, Chapter 6 and Theorem 3.4; DI82 (1.17), Lemmas 2.3 and 3.6; and Kiral–Young, Proposition 3.1 and Corollary 3.2 [15, Chapter 6; Theorem 3.4] [9, (1.17), p. 227; Lemma 2.3, p. 240; Lemma 3.6, p. 247] [18, Proposition 3.1, Corollary 3.2]. These are the conventions used in Paper I, (2.7.T20)–(2.7.T24) and (2.7.T41)–(2.7.T43) [26, (2.7.T20)–(2.7.T24), (2.7.T41)–(2.7.T43), pp. 18–19, 22–23].

4. Finite source identities and decomposition

Throughout this section, NN is an even integer with N≥2N\geq 2. Further size hypotheses appear at each display or just before it. Use L=log⁡NL=\log N from Section 2. We prove the finite identities of this section below. They count each occurrence with its multiplicity. The later analytic estimates are separate hypotheses. Take the roughness cutoff zs=Nαz_{s}=N^{\alpha} from the Root–A scale definition in (6.1). Throughout, nn is a positive source integer. When n∈𝒜Nn\in\mathcal{A}_{N}, n=N−pn=N-p for a prime pp. In a source sum, ee is the integer being counted. The letters p,pi,ai,rp,p_{i},a_{i},r denote prime variables, qq is a positive modulus, and mm is the factor or cofactor specified by its sum. Paper-II counts use n=d⁢mn=dm; the marked count of Section 6 uses m=(N−e)/pm=(N-e)/p. These roles are local to the displayed source. Here Ω⁢(n)\Omega(n) counts prime factors with multiplicity. For squarefree dd with (d,N)=1(d,N)=1, define

Lemma 6.8 (Two-factor convolution estimate).

Let N1/3/8≤H≤2⁢N.46+O⁢(1/L)N^{1/3}/8\leq H\leq 2N^{.46+O(1/L)} and H⁢M≍NHM\asymp N. Proof.

We use the dispersion method of Paper I, Theorem 3.2. It runs on the whole Cartesian shell r∼U1r\sim U_{1}, s∼V1s\sim V_{1}, with residue class Nmodr⁢sN\bmod rs. Its occupied-parent scale conditions are U1≤H⁢N−σpU_{1}\leq HN^{-\sigma_{\mathrm{p}}}, V1≤NvRA+wRA/(H⁢N−σp)V_{1}\leq N^{v_{\mathrm{RA}}+w_{\mathrm{RA}}}/(HN^{-\sigma_{\mathrm{p}}}), and U1⁢V1≤NvRAU_{1}V_{1}\leq N^{v_{\mathrm{RA}}}. The second follows from the displayed bound by D2D_{2} after dropping L−BL^{-B}. The tested sequence is strictly zz-rough. The unary supports carry (r⁢s,N)=1(rs,N)=1 and the individual caps. No pointwise product cap is needed for the rank-one arrays. After Cauchy’s inequality in mm, the split s=d⁢ts=dt above reduces the modulus of the mean square to k=r⁢dk=rd in the range (6.44). The mean square is split at a fixed power of LL below its target. Below it the trivial bound suffices. Above it (6.34) gives (6.35) with a loss of that power, so Lemma 6.5(i) applies. The prime Siegel–Walfisz input is Paper I, (2.21). No joint condition (r,s)=1(r,s)=1 is used, because r,sr,s are not the moduli of Paper I, Theorem 2.8. Write s=d⁢ts=dt as above and k=r⁢dk=rd. A prime p∣(r,s)p\mid(r,s) with p≤zp\leq z divides dd and only enlarges kk. The Chinese remainder step needs only that k,t1,t2k,t_{1},t_{2} are pairwise coprime. The smooth–rough split gives (d,t1⁢t2)=1(d,t_{1}t_{2})=1. A prime p∣(r,s)p\mid(r,s) with p>zp>z divides kk and a rough tit_{i}. Such tuples are the bad type (k,t1⁢t2)>1(k,t_{1}t_{2})>1. If p∣t2p\mid t_{2}, the second progression k⁢t2∣m⁢n2−Nkt_{2}\mid mn_{2}-N places n2n_{2} in one class modulo k⁢pkp. If p∣t1p\mid t_{1} only, exchange the two copies first; the absolute square majorant is symmetric, and the same statement then applies. We therefore remove these tuples before the Chinese remainder step. The cost in the square is ≪M⁢H⁢LC⁢[H/(z⁢K)+1]\ll MHL^{C}[H/(zK)+1]. After the factor K⁢MKM of the first Cauchy step this is ≪N⁢LC⁢(z−1/2+(K/H)1/2)\ll NL^{C}(z^{-1/2}+(K/H)^{1/2}). That is OA⁢(N⁢L−A)O_{A}(NL^{-A}), since z=N1/(log⁡log⁡N)3z=N^{1/(\log\log N)^{3}} and K/H≤N−σp/2K/H\leq N^{-\sigma_{\mathrm{p}}/2}. The zero-mode identity holds for all tuples, including those with gcd failures. After the second Cauchy step, Paper I, Theorem 2.8 bounds the nonzero frequencies. Table B.6 lists the supplementary scripts. The second column states what each one checks. The partitions and defining formulas are printed above. The exact-arithmetic checks use Python’s integer and fraction types. Environment and timing details are recorded in the reproducibility materials. They are not theorem inputs. None replaces an analytic estimate.

The reproducibility verifier checks the recorded inputs and then runs the producer verification. That run regenerates the H6 output, the M5 delay table, the shifted rows and the real inclusion on the recorded platform. The earlier unshifted calculation used Python 3.12.3 and python-flint 0.9.0, with four workers. Its slowest worker took 76397639 seconds, rounded upwards. The historical unshifted comparison is optional and not certified. The main proof does not use it, and it does not affect the shifted computation. Neither these scripts nor their agreement establishes a uniform estimate. The final proof requires the analytic comparisons in Sections 5–8.
